Issued at 215 AM EDT Thu Oct 29 2026

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

Flat mid-level ridging continues to extend from the Gulf into the
Southeast U.S. this morning. A quasi-zonal polar jet extends over
the northern U.S. A weak area of low pressure sits over the Bahamas,
to the south of a sprawling surface high over the Appalachians. A
persistent pressure gradient, responsible for the long duration
of fresh northeasterly flow over the Florida Peninsula, remains
in place. PWAT (moisture) values are still slightly above normal
for late October.

A weak mid-level ridge axis is forecast to move over Florida
late this week, nudging the low farther east and away from
the Bahamas. Behind a jet streak passing over the Great Lakes,
another impressive continental high should be summoned from the
Northern Plains, reaching the Mid-Atlantic states by Saturday
night. This will keep a pressure gradient over Florida through at
least early Monday.

Associated with the subtropical jet, a disorganized pocket of
vorticity currently sits over northern Mexico. Ensemble guidance
suggests this energy will move toward the east, reaching Florida by
Sunday. Expect some interaction with the persistent onshore flow
and moisture; nearly half of the 28/12Z grand ensemble suggests
this outcome.

Mid-level heights are forecast to rise through the middle
of next week, with onshore surface flow continuing but slowly
relaxing. Attention then turns to another disturbance within the
subtropical jet late next week. The latest ensemble clusters show
a trough reaching the Southeast by around next Thursday. Its cold
front may reach the state just beyond the 7-day forecast period,
with unsettled conditions potentially returning at that time.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

Today - Saturday...

Persistence has been the key to the forecast, and we don't see
any wholesale changes as we end the week. We will continue to have
coastal and marine hazards, along with breezy to windy conditions
and periodic showers coming off of the Atlantic.

The highest water levels of this prolonged event appear to be behind
us. This month's king tides begin to diminish as we move past the
full moon. While still gusty, the wind-driven surge lessens a bit
as well. However, minor to moderate coastal flooding remains likely
today, with gradual improvement expected over the next several
high-tide cycles. Peak water levels are anticipated from mid to
late morning before decreasing through the afternoon. Our Coastal
Flood Warning is set to be replaced by a Coastal Flood Advisory
at 2 PM today.

We will keep the High Surf Advisory through this evening as
breakers up to 7 feet remain possible. With numerous rip currents,
interrupted sand bars, erosion, and rough surf, we strongly 
recommend that residents and visitors stay out of the ocean and be
very careful if venturing to our beaches!

Scattered showers remain in the forecast, with a low chance (<25%)
for lightning. A few gusts of 30-35 mph may accompany the heavier
showers. Shower coverage is expected to ramp up on Saturday, and
we will need to monitor for any bands of heavy rain that develop,
especially south of Melbourne.

Outside of any rain, we still forecast occasional wind gusts of
20-30 mph. More breaks of sun are expected, so high temps will
warm back into the low/mid 80s.

Sunday - Monday...

The setup appears favorable for an uptick in rain and even isolated
(20%) lightning coverage. Statistical guidance has already increased
rain chances to 60-80% on Sunday. The deep onshore flow combined
with modest upper jet diffluence is at least somewhat concerning
for the potential of locally heavy rain. This may lead to flooding
of poorly drained areas, especially along the coast on Sunday.

The slow-moving feature begins to exit into the Atlantic on
Monday, but the onshore flow and lingering moisture should provide
above-normal coverage of showers.

Meanwhile, beach conditions are likely to remain hazardous. A
slight uptick in onshore flow may be enough for us to need
another High Surf Advisory for a portion of this period. Either
way, life-threatening rip currents and rough surf are expected
to persist.

Tuesday - next Thursday...

Onshore flow should begin to relax as high pressure nudges over
the peninsula. This allows rain chances to decrease to 20-30% for
the middle of next week. As mentioned in the overview, the next 
signal is a subtropical jet stream disturbance that reaches the 
Southeast U.S. by around next Thursday. Its front may approach the
area by late next Thursday or Friday (11/6), giving us our next 
chance for at least scattered showers and storms. High temps 
should remain warm, in the low/mid 80s.

a threat for strong to severe storms. However, the overall pattern
